questions.q: What was the basic building block of the Mongol decimal military organisation, and how many soldiers did it comprise?
questions.a: The basic building block was the *arban*, comprising 10 soldiers. A wrong answer (e.g., "100 soldiers" or "a tribe") reveals confusion between the decimal units (arban, jaghun, mingghan, tumen) and the older tribal/clan groupings that Genghis Khan deliberately broke up to ensure loyalty to the central command.

questions.q: Why did Genghis Khan replace tribal leadership with a merit-based promotion system within the decimal units?
questions.a: To eliminate tribal fragmentation and ensure absolute loyalty to the Great Khan rather than to clan chiefs. A wrong answer (e.g., "to modernise the army" or "because tribal leaders were incompetent") misses the political motive: the decimal system was a tool of state-building that transformed kinship-based loyalty into institutional loyalty, a concept absent in many contemporary feudal armies.

questions.q: A historian argues that the Mongol "feigned retreat" tactic was merely a copy of earlier steppe nomad practices. Using evidence from the Mongol army's training and coordination, evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The feigned retreat was not a mere copy; the Mongols systematised it through rigorous unit drills (nerge hunts) and integrated it with decimal command signals, allowing entire tumens to execute coordinated feigned retreats and sudden counter-attacks — a level of tactical discipline earlier tribal confederations lacked. A wrong answer that simply agrees shows inability to distinguish between a cultural practice and its institutionalisation into a reproducible military doctrine.

questions.q: Compare the logistical mobility of the Mongol army (multiple remounts per soldier, yam relay stations) with the supply system of the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji (c. 1300 CE). What strategic advantage did the Mongols gain?
questions.a: Each Mongol soldier maintained 3–5 horses, enabling rapid strategic movement (up to 100 km/day) without waiting for supply wagons, while the Sultanate relied on slower baggage trains and fixed granaries. The Mongol advantage was operational tempo: they could concentrate force faster than sedentary armies could react. A wrong answer focusing only on "horses vs. elephants" misses the systemic integration of remounts, yam intelligence, and foraging discipline.

questions.q: Critique the view that Mongol siege warfare succeeded only because they captured Chinese engineers. Assess the role of Mongol adaptability and organisational integration of foreign expertise.
questions.a: While Chinese and Muslim engineers provided technical knowledge (counterweight trebuchets, gunpowder bombs), the Mongol breakthrough was organisational: they created dedicated siege units (nuker), integrated engineers into the decimal chain of command, and used mobility to isolate fortresses before assault. A wrong answer that attributes success solely to "foreign technology" overlooks the Mongol capacity to institutionalise and scale borrowed innovations — a pattern also seen in their adoption of Uyghur script and Persian administration.

questions.q: Construct a historical argument explaining how the keshig (imperial guard) functioned simultaneously as a military elite, a training academy for commanders, and a political instrument of central control.
questions.a: A strong answer will link three functions: (1) the keshig was the most loyal tumen, directly answerable to the Khan; (2) its members were drawn from aristocratic families as hostages and from meritorious commoners, creating a mixed elite bonded to the Khan; (3) keshig officers were rotated to field commands, spreading standardized doctrine. A poor answer lists only one function or treats the keshig as merely a bodyguard unit, missing its role in replicating the central military culture across the empire.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Mongol Army (1206–1368 CE) was a highly ______, decimal-based military force organized into units of 10 (arban), 100 (jaghun), 1,000 (mingghan), and 10,000 (tumen), which combined steppe mobility, composite bow mastery, and innovative siege tactics to conquer Eurasia under Genghis Khan and his successors.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are visiting the Qutb Minar complex in Delhi and notice the Iron Pillar ______ since the Gupta period.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the decimal organisation, merit-based promotion, and specialised tactics (feigned retreat, encirclement, siege engineering) interacted to create a military system that outperformed larger sedentary armies, and can compare its logistical mobility with contemporary Indian sultanate armies.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ the Qutb Minar complex in Delhi and notice the Iron Pillar standing since the Gupta period.
